amstar2_items.justification: No PICO components (population, intervention/exposure, comparator, outcome) are formulated; the review addresses a broad policy question on improving rural US water supply and explicitly includes both empirical and non-empirical sources.
No pre-registered or a priori review protocol is reported or referenced, and no protocol deviations are discussed.

The author states that both empirical and non-empirical sources were chosen while simultaneously asserting they had to use quantitative analytical approaches (p. 4), providing no coherent methodological rationale for study-design eligibility and citing blog posts, books, and conceptual essays.

Although multiple databases and general search terms are listed (pp. 3-4), no reproducible search strings are provided, no reference-list or expert searches are reported, and sources were arbitrarily filtered by selecting journals with the largest impact factors in Web of Science and restricting to public administration and social sciences without methodological justification.
Single-authored review with no independent duplicate screening reported.
Single-authored review with no independent duplicate data extraction reported.

Inline narrative descriptions do not systematically report primary study designs, sample sizes, interventions, comparators, or outcomes, Table 1 (pp. 5-7) is rendered as an unindexed image in the PDF text layer, and numerous inline citations misattribute unrelated non-US or conceptual papers to US rural water statistics.
The text reports excluding 10 duplicates and 19 screened papers out of 65 records (p. 8), but provides no bibliographic list of excluded full-text studies or study-specific exclusion justifications.
No risk-of-bias or methodological quality assessment tool was applied to individual included studies; only journal impact factors in Web of Science were checked (p. 4).
Sources of funding for the included studies are not reported anywhere in the review.
No quantitative synthesis or meta-analysis was performed; findings are summarized strictly as a thematic narrative essay.
Risk of bias in individual studies was neither assessed nor accounted for when interpreting findings and formulating policy recommendations.
Heterogeneity in study designs, geographies, or findings across included works is neither systematically analyzed nor explained.
No quantitative synthesis was performed, and publication bias was not investigated.
No conflict-of-interest statement or review funding disclosure is reported in the article.

methodological_notes: Although the author self-describes the paper as a PRISMA 'systematic review' (pp. 1, 3) reporting 65 identified records, 10 duplicates removed, 19 excluded at screening, and 36 included documents (p. 8), the study is methodologically a single-author pseudo-systematic narrative essay of Critically Low quality under AMSTAR 2. First, no protocol, PICO framework, duplicate screening/extraction, excluded-study list, risk-of-bias appraisal, or conflict-of-interest disclosure is provided, and candidate journals were arbitrarily filtered by Web of Science impact factor (p. 4). Second, eligibility criteria are internally contradictory—claiming 'Both empirical and non-empirical sources were chosen' while immediately requiring 'quantitative approaches on the issue at hand with an analytical rather than descriptive methodology' and data 'taken from the US government' (p. 4)—yet the synthesis relies heavily on Gizmodo/ScienceDaily news posts, books, UN/WHO reports, conceptual essays, and secondary reviews (e.g., Llausàs & Saurí 2017; March et al. 2012; Rozema et al. 2016; Saurí 2013). Third, Table 1 ('Literature analyzed', pp. 5-7) was embedded as a non-OCR raster image in the source PDF so its 36 rows are blank in extracted text; meanwhile, 52 distinct works are cited across the thematic synthesis sections (pp. 8-13, extracted above separately from Introduction-only citations), with pervasive citation misattribution (e.g., citing Spanish conservation-theatre, EU 30% climate-target, and Australian suburban-garden studies for US rural aquifer, Florida wastewater, and California desalination claims). Substantively, it is borderline on narrow Criterion 2 because it discusses public vs. investor-owned/cooperative/self-supply ownership, reserved water rights, regulatory oversight, tariffs/cost recovery, and federal farm-bill conservation subsidies, but conflates agricultural land-stewardship programs (CSP, EQIP) with household rural drinking-water governance without rigorous empirical synthesis.
review_design_self_description: Self-described PRISMA systematic review (in practice a hybrid/pseudo-systematic qualitative narrative policy review including both empirical and non-empirical sources)
